books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, B. Advances in Technology
Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, D. Regional Specialization
The North and the Textile Industry

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note); Lowell Offering wording verified against the Project Gutenberg text
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which industrialization changed the daily lives of American workers in the period 1800-1848.

documents.title: The first power loom
documents.source: Account of the first power loom in the United States, 1813, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the power loom that let American mills make finished cloth in the factory.
documents.text: The first power loom, built in 1813, meant that textile manufacturers could produce both thread and finished fabric in their own factories, quickly and cheaply. Women who had woven their own cloth at home began to buy cloth instead.

documents.title: The Waltham-Lowell system
documents.source: Description of the Waltham-Lowell system, 1810s, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the factory system developed in Waltham and Lowell, Massachusetts.
documents.text: The Waltham-Lowell system brought all stages of textile production under one roof, with employees living in company housing. Mill owners recruited young women from nearby farms, paid them cash wages, and housed them in chaperoned boardinghouses.

documents.title: The Lowell mill girls turn out
documents.source: Account of the Lowell turn-out of 1834, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the strike by Lowell mill women against a wage cut.
documents.text: In 1834, when the Lowell mills cut wages, hundreds of mill girls walked out of the mills in protest, marching together through the town. The turn-out showed that wage workers could act together against their employers, though the mills soon replaced them.

documents.title: The ten-hour day
documents.source: Account of the ten-hour movement, 1836, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the campaign by industrial workers for shorter working hours.
documents.text: In the 1830s, industrial workers began calling on state legislatures to limit the working day. Mill hands commonly worked eleven to thirteen hours a day, and the ten-hour movement asked for a shorter day so workers would have time for rest and study.

documents.title: The ten-hour day for federal workers
documents.source: President Martin Van Buren's executive order, 1840, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The president's order setting hours for workers on federal projects.
documents.text: In 1840, President Martin Van Buren ordered a ten-hour working day for laborers on federal public works. The order answered the workers' campaign, though it covered only federal projects and not the private mills where most factory hands worked.

documents.title: Mill women defend their work
documents.source: Dignity of Labor, The Lowell Offering, 1842, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An essay by the young women working in the Lowell textile mills, defending wage labor.
documents.text: "From whence originated the idea, that it was derogatory to a lady's dignity, or a blot upon the female character, to labor? . . . Few American fortunes will support a woman who is above the calls of her family. . . . To be able to earn one's own living by laboring with the hands, should be reckoned among female accomplishments."

documents.title: The steel plow
documents.source: Account of John Deere's steel plow, 1837, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the plow Deere developed for prairie farming.
documents.text: John Deere's steel plow, developed in 1837, proved more durable and efficient than the cast-iron plow. It cut through thick prairie soil, letting farm families work more land with fewer hands and sell more grain to distant markets.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which industrialization changed the daily lives of American workers, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the cutoff of British imports during the Embargo and the War of 1812, or the growth of a national market after 1815.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the limits of the change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Panic of 1819, the Tariff of 1816, or the Waltham-Lowell system.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where the market revolution transformed the economy and where older ways persisted.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Industrialization changed workers' daily lives to a great extent: it moved work from the home to the factory clock, gave young women cash wages and a life of their own, and taught workers to act together, but long hours and low pay stayed, and most Americans still farmed.
Context: Before factories, most manufacturing was home piecework under the putting-out system, and most Americans farmed for their families. The cutoff of British goods during the embargo and the War of 1812 pushed manufacturing into American mills.
Grouping: Documents 1 and 2 show the new factory and its workforce; Documents 3, 4, and 5 show workers answering with protest and the ten-hour campaign; Documents 6 and 7 show how workers judged their new lives and how farm work changed too.
Beyond the documents: By the early 1840s, over 75,000 workers, nearly half of them women, worked in American textile mills; the Lowell system lasted until Irish immigration in the 1840s and 1850s made factory labor plentiful.
Complexity: The change was real but mixed: mill work gave farm daughters wages and independence, yet it also set their hours by the factory bell and cut their pay when the mills chose.
